topics.title: Force a collision history rather than hoping for one
topics.summary: The collision laboratory deliberately gives every key the same probe origin. Its seven-slot capacity is fixed, and it makes no average-case hashing-performance claim. This is an adversarial correctness arrangement: every lookup must respect the sequence of occupied, deleted, and never-used slots.

The independent std::map model expresses membership and values without sharing that probe mechanism.

reading.title: Force a collision history rather than hoping for one
paragraphs: The collision laboratory deliberately gives every key the same probe origin. Its seven-slot capacity is fixed, and it makes no average-case hashing-performance claim. This is an adversarial correctness arrangement: every lookup must respect the sequence of occupied, deleted, and never-used slots.

An update must continue past a deleted slot because the key may already exist later in the probe path. The implementation remembers the first reusable position but does not commit a new key until it knows whether an existing key should be updated. The independent std::map model expresses membership and values without sharing that probe mechanism.

The generated history mixes insertion, update, deletion, full-table rejection, and reads over thirteen possible keys. After each operation, every key in that bounded universe is compared. A full table must still permit updating an existing key. A failed insertion of a new key must leave all accepted associations unchanged.

To extend this lab, record the operation list and add a reducer that removes contiguous blocks while preserving a failure. Keep the reference policy bounded to seven accepted distinct keys; comparing with an unbounded map without that policy would make full-table rejection look incorrectly like a defect.

topics.title: Return a BFS witness and replace recursive DFS frames explicitly
topics.summary: The graph laboratory produces one shortest unweighted path and detects directed cycles without recursive calls. BFS records a predecessor only at first discovery. Marking discovery before enqueueing ensures that another edge cannot enqueue the same vertex as a fresh discovery. The selected path depends on adjacency order; the contract does not claim a unique path when several shortest paths exist.

blocks.headingContext: Return a BFS witness and replace recursive DFS frames explicitly

blocks.text: The DFS frame stores both the current vertex and the next neighbor index. That index is the continuation state a recursive call would have retained. Gray means active in the current depth-first chain; black means fully processed. An edge to a gray vertex establishes a directed cycle, while an edge to a black vertex can simply converge on already completed work.

blocks.headingContext: Return a BFS witness and replace recursive DFS frames explicitly

blocks.text: The reference to the top frame is not used after a push_back that might reallocate the frame vector. This is an ownership and invalidation issue inside an algorithm often described only in graph terms. The twenty-thousand-vertex chain test demonstrates that this implementation does not consume one native recursive call per vertex; it still allocates explicit storage proportional to depth.

topics.title: Make stability observable with record identities
topics.summary: Sorting integers alone cannot reveal whether equal records exchanged positions. The stability lab pairs each key with an arrival identity. Its merge chooses from the left half whenever the keys are equal, preserving the relative order inherited from the original sequence.

blocks.text: The test compares complete records with std::stable_sort, then separately checks nondecreasing keys and increasing arrival identities within equal-key groups. The second check directly expresses stability rather than trusting only equality with a library result. Empty, repeated, negative, and mixed keys arise in the bounded deterministic trial set.

topics.title: Compare a recurrence with an independent state-space search
topics.summary: The coin laboratory compares bottom-up minimum-count tabulation with breadth-first traversal of reachable amounts. A BFS edge means adding one allowed denomination. Because every edge uses one coin, the number of layers to the target is the minimum count. This is a different evaluation model from the table recurrence, although both depend on the same stated unbounded positive-denomination problem.

blocks.text: The lab enumerates all subsets of denominations one through six and targets zero through forty. It also checks the familiar non-greedy example and invalid inputs. The table’s sentinel is safe under the explicit target limit of one hundred; it must not be copied into an unbounded cost problem without reconsidering arithmetic and reachability.

blocks.text: The enumeration is exhaustive over that selected small universe, not over every integer input. Its value is that boundary states, disconnected reachable sets, empty choices, and noncanonical denomination combinations are exercised systematically. Preserve those limits in the report so a finite experiment remains useful evidence rather than an exaggerated universal claim.
